first_fatal_gap.description: The candidate claims that the geometric overlap condition for two δ-tubes—a + t₁θ₁ ≈ b + t₂θ₂, which is a 4-ary relation in the independent parameters (a, θ₁, b, θ₂)—can be encoded as a bipartite graph G ⊂ A × B with A = {intercepts} and B = {shifted directions tθ}. This is structurally impossible: G ⊂ A × B is a binary relation and cannot capture the simultaneous dependence on two intercepts and two directions. The candidate never defines a map from ordered pairs of tubes into A × B, never proves that membership (a, b) ∈ G is equivalent to geometric overlap, and never justifies the assertion that the sumset {a + b : (a, b) ∈ G} counts distinct spatial overlap regions. In fact, a + b mixes an intercept from one tube with a direction parameter from another tube, which has no geometric interpretation as an overlap location; likewise, a − b does not reproduce the stated overlap equation without additional unmotivated constraints. Because the hypotheses of the Katz–Tao sum-difference lemma are not satisfied, the combinatorial engine cannot be engaged. The step further lacks any quantified dependence between δ and N, any epsilon bookkeeping, and any treatment of exceptional configurations (e.g., nearly parallel tubes or intercepts near grid boundaries).

D.notes: The proof collapses at its purported bridge between continuous geometry and additive combinatorics. Prior to Step 3 the argument is merely incomplete; in Step 3 the candidate presents an incoherent algebraic formalization that cannot support any subsequent t-discretization, slice summation, or volume estimate. All later steps depend on this unfounded identification and are therefore moot. No polynomial loss factors in δ are tracked, no disjointness or overcounting analysis for the sets G_j can salvage the argument, and no exceptional configurations are handled.

evidence.description: The bound (4n+3)/7 for the Minkowski dimension of Kakeya sets and the additive-combinatorics approach using sum-difference estimates were established in the early 2000s.
Recent literature surveys the Katz-Tao arithmetic Kakeya framework and notes that the core sum-difference bound has remained unchanged for over 20 years, confirming the approach is well-established.
Katz explicitly discussed the sum-differences method in the context of Kakeya problems, ruling out elementary variants but cementing the approach as classical literature.

E.notes: The submission reconstructs the classical Katz-Tao arithmetic combinatorics route to Kakeya bounds: discretizing tubes into a δ-grid, mapping geometric overlaps to sum/difference sets, and invoking the Katz-Tao sum-difference lemma to obtain the bound (4n+3)/7 (15/7 for n=3). This strategy, including the specific exponent and intercept-sum identity, has been known since the early 2000s (e.g., arXiv:0102135). The proof_graph.json even lists arXiv:0102135 as a retrieved dependency, confirming the submission is drawn from existing literature rather than an independent novel route.
